09 Modelling, Visualising and Analysing Network Data with R

Author

Yiqiong PAN

Published

March 11, 2026

Modified

March 12, 2026

1 Overview

In this hands on exercise, we learn how to model, analyse and visualise network data using R.

By the end of this exercise, we will be able to:

  • construct graph objects from data frames and manipulate them using functions from dplyr, lubridate, and tidygraph

  • create network visualisations using functions from the ggraph package

  • compute network metrics and structural properties using tidygraph

  • develop more advanced network visualisations by incorporating network metrics into the graph design

  • build interactive network visualisations using the visNetwork package

2 Getting Started

2.1 Installing and Loading Packages

In this hands on exercise, four R packages for network modelling and visualisation will be installed and loaded. These packages are igraph, tidygraph, ggraph, and visNetwork.

In addition, the tidyverse collection of packages and lubridate, which is designed for handling and manipulating date and time data in R, will also be installed and loaded.

Package Description
tidyverse A collection of R packages for data importing, cleaning, transformation, and visualisation (e.g., readr, dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2).
igraph Creats and analyses graphs and networks.
tidygraph Provides a tidy interface for working with graph and network data in R.
visNetwork Provides an R interface to the vis.js JavaScript library for network visualisation.
ggraph ggplot2 extension for visualising graphs and networks.
graphlayouts Provides additional layout algorithms for network visualisation that are not available in igraph
clock Provides a comprehensive toolkit for working with date and time data in R.
lubridate A Tidyverse package that handles date-time objects
concaveman Offers a very fast algorithm for computing 2D concave hulls from a set of points
ggforce Extends ggplot2 with additional statistical transformations and geometric layers for creating more specialised visualisations. 
pacman::p_load(igraph, tidygraph, ggraph, 
               visNetwork, lubridate, clock,
               tidyverse, graphlayouts, 
               concaveman, ggforce)

3 The Data

The datasets used in this exercise come from an oil exploration and extraction company. One dataset contains node data, while the other contains edge (link) data describing the relationships between nodes.

3.3 Importing network data from files

We import GAStech-email_edges.csv and GAStech_email_nodes.csv into RStudio environment by using read_csv() of readr package.

GAStech_nodes <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_node.csv")
GAStech_edges <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv")

3.5 Wrangling time

The code below converts the SentDate values into day month year format and creates a new column called weekday based on the SentDate column. This is done using the dmy() and wday() functions from the lubridate package, with weekday names in ordinal scale and disabled in abbreviated form.

GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(SentDate,
                        label = TRUE,abbr = FALSE))

3.7 Wrangling attributes

A closer look at the GAStech_edges data frame shows that it contains individual email flow records, which are not very suitable for visualisation.

To make the data more useful, we will aggregate the records by date, sender, receiver, main subject, and day of the week.

The code blow first filters work related emails, groups the data by source (sender), target (receiver) and weekday (day the email sent), counts the number of emails for each sender receiver weekday combination and stores the results in a new variable called weight, removes emails from themselves, the finally removes grouping so the data can be used normally in later analysis or visualisation.

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
    summarise(Weight = n()) %>%
  filter(source!=target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

4 Creating Network Objects Using tidygraph

In this section, we learn how to create a graph data model using the tidygraph package. It provides a tidy API for graph and network manipulation. Although network data is not naturally tidy, it can be represented as two tidy tables: one containing node data and the other containing edge data.

The tidygraph package allows users to switch between these two tables and apply familiar dplyr verbs to manipulate them. It also provides access to many graph algorithms whose outputs integrate well within a tidy workflow.

Before getting started, we could read the following two articles:

  • Introducing tidygraph

  • tidygraph 1.1 - A tidy hope

4.1 The tbl_graph object

The tidygraph package provides two functions for creating network objects:

  • tbl_graph() creates a tbl_graph network object from node and edge data.

  • as_tbl_graph() converts existing network data or objects into a tbl_graph network.

The as_tbl_graph() function supports several data formats, including:

  • a node data frame and an edge data frame
  • data frame, list, or matrix from base R
  • igraph objects
  • network objects
  • dendrogram and hclust objects from stats
  • Node objects from data.tree
  • phylo and evonet objects from ape
  • graphNEL, graphAM, and graphBAM objects from the graph package in Bioconductor

4.2 dplyr verbs in tidygraph

The activate() function in tidygraph is used to switch between the node and edge tables in a tbl_graph object. Any dplyr verbs applied to the tbl_graph will operate on the currently active table.

iris_tree <- iris_tree %>% 
    activate(nodes) %>% 
    mutate(Species = ifelse(leaf, as.character(iris$Species)[label], NA)) %>% 
    activate(edges) %>% 
    mutate(to_setose = .N()$Species[to] == 'setosa')
iris_tree

When working with edges, the helper functions can be used to access different parts of the graph:

  • .N() returns the node data
  • .E() returns the edge data
  • .G() returns the entire tbl_graph object

4.3 Using tbl_graph() to build tidygraph data model

The code below uses tbl_graph() of tidygraph package to build an tidygraph’s network graph data.frame. The aggregated edges dataset is passed to the edges argument, and directed = TRUE specifies that the network is directed, meaning the relationships have a direction (for example, emails sent from a sender to a receiver).

GAStech_graph <- tbl_graph(nodes = GAStech_nodes,
                           edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated, 
                           directed = TRUE)

It also indicates that the node data is active. In a tbl_graph object, only one tibble (nodes or edges) is active at a time, allowing users to manipulate each table separately.

4.5 Changing the active object

The nodes tibble is activated by default in a tbl_graph object. However, the active table can be changed using the activate() function.

For example, if we want to rearrange the rows in the edges tibble so that edges with the highest weight appear first, we can first activate the edges table and then apply desc() order in arrange() function.

The output below shows the rearranged edge tibble.

GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(edges) %>%
  arrange(desc(Weight))

5 Plotting Static Network Graphs with ggraph Package

ggraph is an extension of ggplot2 that allows users to apply familiar ggplot2 concepts when creating network graphs.

A network graph created with ggraph has three main components:

  • nodes
  • edges
  • layouts

Nodes represent the entities in the network, edges represent the relationships between them, and layouts determine how the nodes and edges are arranged visually in the graph.

For a more detailed explanation of these components, please refer to the relevant ggraph vignettes.

5.1 Plotting a basic network graph

The code chunk below uses ggraph(), geom_edge_link(), and geom_node_point() to plot a network graph using GAStech_graph.

ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point()
Tip

  • The basic plotting function is ggraph(), which takes the network data and the desired layout type as inputs.

  • Since it is built on igraph, ggraph() can work with either an igraph object or a tbl_graph object.

  • The function takes “stress” as default layout.

5.2 Changing the default network graph theme

The code below uses theme_graph() to remove the x and y axes.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes()) +
  geom_node_point(aes())

g + theme_graph()

th_no_axes() removes axis lines, tick marks and axis labels.

ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point() +
  labs(title = "GAStech Email Network") +
  theme_graph(background = scales::alpha("red", 0.2)) +
  th_no_axes()
Tip

ggraph provides a ggplot theme called theme_graph(), which is designed for network visualisations. It removes axes, grid lines, and borders, and sets the default font to Arial Narrow (which can be customised).

The theme can be applied in two ways:

  • Use set_graph_style() to apply the style to multiple plots.
  • Use theme_graph() within an individual plot.

5.3 Changing the coloring of the plot

We can customise the colouring of edge, node and background by using theme_graph().

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(colour = 'grey50')) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = 'grey40'))

g + theme_graph(background = 'grey10',
                text_colour = 'white')

When a value is placed inside aes(), ggplot assumes it is a mapped variable, not a fixed colour. Even though grey50 is just a string, ggplot treats it as a category, so it automatically creates a legend. Since it thinks it is a categorical variable, it automatically assigns colours from the default ggplot palette, where the first colour is often red.

To actually use the grey colour, we must place it outside aes():

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph) +
  geom_edge_link(colour = "grey50", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(colour = "grey40", size = 2)

g +
  labs(title = "GAStech Email Network") +
  theme_graph(background = "grey10",
              text_colour = "white")

5.4 Working with ggraph’s layouts

ggraph supports many commonly used network layouts, including star, circle, nicely (default), dh, gem, graphopt, grid, mds, sphere, randomly, fr, kk, drl, and lgl.

The figures below and on the right illustrate several layouts supported by ggraph().

5.5 Fruchterman and Reingold layout

The code chunks below will be used to plot the network graph using Fruchterman and Reingold layout. The layout is most widely used force directed layout and a good general purpose network layout.

ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(size = 2) +
  theme_graph()

5.6 Nicely layout

The default layout. It automatically selects a suitable layout.

ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_node_point(size = 2) +
  theme_graph(background = "lightgreen")

5.7 Modifying network nodes

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") + 
  geom_edge_link() +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), size = 3)

g + theme_graph(text_colour = "blue")
Tip

  • aes(colour = Department) maps node colour to department, so each department gets a different colour.

  • size = 3 controls the node size.

  • theme_graph(text_colour = "blue") changes the plot text colour (titles, legend text) to blue.

5.8 Modifying edges

The code below maps the thickness of the edges with the Weight variable.

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "kk") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), colour = "grey",
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 3)

g + theme_graph(text_colour = "white",background = "black")
Tip

  • geom_edge_link() draws edges as straight lines between the start and end nodes. It can also map visual properties to edge attributes.

  • For example, the width argument can map the line thickness to the Weight attribute, and the alpha argument controls the opacity of the edges.

6 Creating Facet Graphs

Another useful feature of ggraph is faceting. In network visualisation, faceting helps reduce edge overplotting by separating nodes and edges into different panels based on their attributes.

There are three faceting functions in ggraph:

  • facet_nodes() draws edges in a panel only when both connected nodes are present in that panel.
  • facet_edges() always draws all nodes in every panel, even if the faceting variable belongs to the edges.
  • facet_graph() allows faceting by two variables simultaneously, typically one for nodes and one for edges.

6.1 Working with facet_edges()

The code below create network graph by using facet_edges().

First we apply default ggraph them for network plots by using set_graph_style() to remove axes and grids. They we create a base graph by using ggraph() on tl_graph object, then we draw the edges between nodes by mapping the thickness of the edge to the number of emails exchanged (Weight variable) and control the edge widths so they vary between 0.1 to 5 by using scale_edge_width(). We then colour the nodes to indicate department and control the node size. Finally we creates seperate panels for each weekday by using facet_edges().

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "nicely") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~Weekday, ncol = 2, scales = "free")

Similarly, we can also create a network plot based on email contents.

GAStech_edges_aggregated_subject <- GAStech_edges %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday, MainSubject) %>%
  summarise(Weight = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1)

GAStech_graph_subject <- tbl_graph(nodes = GAStech_nodes,
                           edges = GAStech_edges_aggregated_subject, 
                           directed = TRUE)
set_graph_style()


g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph_subject, 
            layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~MainSubject)
Tip
  • Key Arguments for facet_edges()

-nrow, ncol: control the number of rows and columns of the facet panels.

  • scales controls whether the axis scales are shared or independent across panels. Options: "fixed" (default):same scale for all panels; "free": scales vary; "free_x": x scale varies; "free_y": y scale varies

  • labellercontrols how facet labels are displayed (e.g., formatting of panel titles)

-drop: If TRUE, unused factor levels are removed from the facets.

  • dir controls the direction of panel arrangement (“h”, “v”, “lt”, “tl”, “lb”, “bl”, “rt”, “tr”, “rb”, or “br”).

  • strip.position: controls where the facet labels appear (top, bottom, left, or right).

-facet_edges() works like facet_wrap() but only facets edges. Nodes are repeated in every panel.

6.2 Working with facet_edges()

The code below uses theme() to change the position and size of the legend.

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "nicely") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 2) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6)
  )
  
g + facet_edges(~Weekday)

6.3 A framed facet graph

The th_foreground() function adds a foreground title to each facet panel, draws a frame around the panels, and allows the foreground text colour to be controlled using the fg_text_colour argument.

set_graph_style()
g<- ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 2)

g + facet_edges(~Weekday) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "gray80", border = TRUE, fg_text_colour = "brown") +
  theme(legend.position = "top",legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.title = element_text(size = 8))

6.4 Working with facet_nodes()

The code demonstrates the usage of facet_nodes().

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "nicely") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 2)
  
g + facet_nodes(~Department, ncol = 2, dir = "v", strip.position = "bottom")+
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80",  
                border = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom',legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.title = element_text(size = 8))
Tip

  • Key arguments for facet_nodes()

  • quite similar to facet_edges()

-nrow, ncol: control the number of rows and columns of the facet panels.

  • scales controls whether the axis scales are shared or independent across panels. Options: "fixed" (default):same scale for all panels; "free": scales vary; "free_x": x scale varies; "free_y": y scale varies

  • labellercontrols how facet labels are displayed (e.g., formatting of panel titles)

-drop: If TRUE, unused factor levels are removed from the facets.

  • dir controls the direction of panel arrangement (“h”, “v”, “lt”, “tl”, “lb”, “bl”, “rt”, “tr”, “rb”, or “br”).

  • strip.position: controls where the facet labels appear (top, bottom, left, or right).

-facet_nodes() facets based on node attributes. Edges are only drawn if both connected nodes appear in that panel.

6.5 Working with facet_graph()

set_graph_style()

g <- ggraph(GAStech_graph, 
            layout = "nicely") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), 
                  size = 2)
  
set_graph_style()  # Sets a default graph style/theme


g + 
  facet_graph(Weekday ~ Department,  # The faceting formula
    row_type = "edge",  # Facet rows by edge attribute (Weekday)
    col_type = "node"   # Facet columns by node attribute (Department)
  ) +
  th_foreground(foreground = "grey80", border = TRUE) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

7 Network Metrics Analysis

7.1 Computing centrality indices

Centrality measures are statistical indices used to describe the relative importance of actors in a network. Four commonly used centrality measures are degree, betweenness, closeness, and eigenvector centrality.

  • Degree centrality: centrality_degree()

Measures the number of direct connections a node has. Nodes with higher degree interact with more actors in the network.

  • Betweenness: centrality_betweenness() Measures how often a node lies on the shortest paths between other nodes. Nodes with high betweenness often act as bridges or intermediaries.

  • Closeness: centrality_closeness() Measures how close a node is to all other nodes in the network based on the shortest paths. Nodes with high closeness can reach others more quickly.

  • Eigenvector centrality: centrality_eigen() Measures a node’s importance based on both its connections and the importance of the nodes it connects to. Nodes connected to influential nodes receive higher scores.

The principles and mathematical details of these measures are beyond the scope of this hands on exercise. Students are encouraged to refer to Chapter 7: Actor Prominence in A User’s Guide to Network Analysis in R for a deeper understanding of these concepts.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department,
            size=betweenness_centrality))
g + theme_graph() + theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"))
Tip

  • The mutate() function from dplyr is used to compute and add new variables to the graph data.

  • In this case, the centrality_betweenness() function from tidygraph is used to calculate the betweenness centrality of each node.

7.2 Visualising network metrics

From ggraph version 2.0 onward, algorithms from tidygraph, such as centrality measures, can be used directly within ggraph plotting calls. This means that it is no longer necessary to precompute and store centrality values in the graph object before using them in a visualisation.

The first plot uses the size = centrality_betweenness() for the nodes while the second plot uses centrality_eigen().

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, 
                      size = centrality_betweenness()))
g + theme_graph()+ theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"))
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(aes(width=Weight), 
                 alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, 
                      size = centrality_eigen()))
g + theme_graph()+ theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"))

7.3 Visualising Community

The tidygraph package inherits many community detection algorithms from igraph and makes them available for network analysis. These include Edge betweenness (group_edge_betweenness()), Leading eigenvector (group_leading_eigen()), Fast greedy (group_fast_greedy()), Louvain (group_louvain()), Walktrap (group_walktrap()), Label propagation (group_label_prop()), InfoMAP (group_infomap()), Spinglass (group_spinglass()), and Optimal (group_optimal()).

Some of these algorithms consider edge direction or weight, while others ignore them. For more details, refer to the documentation on community detection functions provided by tidygraph.

In the code chunk below, the group_edge_betweenness() function is used to detect communities in the network.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight, 
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") + 
  geom_edge_link(
    aes(
      width=Weight), 
    alpha=0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(
    range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(colour = community), size =3)  

g + theme_graph( background = "beige",text_colour = "brown")+ theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm"))

Here we try out the Louvain method: most popular for large networks.

GAStech_graph_undirected <- GAStech_graph %>%
  convert(to_undirected)

g <- GAStech_graph_undirected %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(group_louvain(weights = Weight))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community), size = 4)

g + 
  theme_graph(base_family = "sans") +
  theme(
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6),
    legend.key.size = unit(0.4, "cm")
  )

To support more effective visual investigation, the community network above has been enhanced using geom_mark_hull() from the ggforce package. This function highlights clusters by drawing hulls around groups of nodes.

Before running the code chunk below, ensure that the ggforce and concaveman packages are installed and loaded.

After activating the node table stored in the tbl_graph object, the function group_optimal() from the tidygraph package is used to detect communities (clusters) in the network. Nodes that interact more frequently are grouped into the same community. The weights argument refers to the email communication frequency, and the community labels are converted into factors so they can be mapped to colours in the visualisation.

Next, betweenness centrality is computed for each node. Nodes with high betweenness lie on many shortest paths between other nodes and often act as bridges connecting different groups in the network.

The network is then visualised using the Fruchterman Reingold layout (fr), a force directed layout where strongly connected nodes move closer together, while weakly connected nodes move further apart.

The geom_mark_hull() function from the ggforce package is used to draw community boundaries, creating shaded polygons around nodes belonging to the same community. In this function, group = community groups nodes by community, fill = community assigns different colours to each community, alpha controls the transparency, expand adjusts the space around the nodes, and radius smooths the edges of the polygons.

Finally, edges are drawn using geom_edge_link() and nodes are plotted using geom_node_point(), and a network theme theme_graph() is applied to produce a cleaner and more visually appealing graph.

The concaveman package is used internally by geom_mark_hull() to compute concave hull polygons that outline the boundaries of communities in the network.

g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(
    community = as.factor(group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
    betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()
  ) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x = x, y = y, group = community, fill = community),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(
    aes(fill = Department, size = betweenness_measure),
    colour = "black",
    shape = 21
  )

g + theme_graph( background = "beige",text_colour = "brown")+ theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 6), legend.key.size = unit(0.3, "cm"), legend.title = element_text(size = 8))

8 Building Interactive Network Graph with visNetwork

visNetwork is an R package for network visualisation that uses the vis.js JavaScript library.

  • The visNetwork() function creates an interactive network graph using a nodes list and an edges list.

    • The nodes list must contain an id column, while the edges list must include from and to columns to define the connections between nodes.

    • Node labels are displayed using the label column in the node list.

  • The resulting graph is fun to play around with.

    • Users can drag nodes, and the layout algorithm will automatically adjust their positions.

    • It also allows users to zoom in and out and move the graph to explore different parts of the network.

8.1 Data preparation

Before we can plot the interactive network graph, we need to prepare the data model by using the code chunk below. This code prepares the edge list for the visNetwork graph by matching employee names with their node IDs and aggregating email interactions.

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("sourceLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(from = id) %>%
  left_join(GAStech_nodes, by = c("targetLabel" = "label")) %>%
  rename(to = id) %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(from, to) %>%
    summarise(weight = n()) %>%
  filter(from!=to) %>%
  filter(weight > 1) %>%
  ungroup()

8.2 Working with layout

This code creates an interactive network graph using the visNetwork package and applies a Fruchterman Reingold layout to position the nodes.

The visNetwork() function builds the network graph using: GAStech_nodes,the nodes list, containing information about each employee (such as id, label, department),GAStech_edges_aggregated the edges list containing information about from, to, weight.visIgraphLayout() applies a graph layout.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr")

8.3 Working with visual attributes: Nodes

The visNetwork() function automatically looks for a column named group in the nodes dataset and colours the nodes based on the values in that column.

In the code below, the Department field is renamed to group.

GAStech_nodes <- GAStech_nodes %>%
  rename(group = Department)

When the network is plotted again, visNetwork assigns different colours to the nodes according to their group categories, allowing each department to be visually distinguished in the network graph.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

8.4 Working with visual attributes: Edges

In the code below, visEdges() is used to customise the appearance of the edges in the network graph.

  • The arrows argument specifies where arrows should appear on the edges, indicating the direction of the connection.
  • The smooth argument draws the edges as curved lines instead of straight lines, which helps improve readability when many edges overlap.
visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visEdges(arrows = "to", 
           smooth = list(enabled = TRUE, 
                         type = "curvedCW")) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)

More customisation options can be found here.

8.5 Interactivity

In the code chunk below, visOptions() is used to add interactive features to the network visualisation.

  • The highlightNearest argument highlights the nodes that are closest to the selected node when it is clicked.

  • The nodesIdSelection argument adds a node selection menu, creating an HTML drop down list that allows users to select and highlight a specific node in the network.

visNetwork(GAStech_nodes,
           GAStech_edges_aggregated) %>%
  visIgraphLayout(layout = "layout_with_fr") %>%
  visOptions(highlightNearest = TRUE,
             nodesIdSelection = TRUE) %>%
  visLegend() %>%
  visLayout(randomSeed = 123)
